medical.title: Tuberculosis rapid test allows in-the-field results
medical.summary: Northwestern University engineers have developed a new way to quickly test for tuberculosis that avoids several pitfalls of other methods.

medical.title: Protein guides cytoneme 'highway' formation to support developmental signaling
medical.summary: Cytonemes are tendril-like appendages that developing cells use to communicate across large distances. Their cargo—including the key signaling protein Sonic Hedgehog (SHH)—is highly specific, but the mechanisms underlying this specificity were unclear.

medical.title: 7 simple self-care habits that may ease anxiety and depression
medical.summary: If you've been feeling more on edge lately, you're far from alone.

medical.title: How to test whether brain organoids possess consciousness
medical.summary: The development of brain organoids is advancing at a breakneck pace. Researchers are creating tiny cell clusters in the lab that behave like fragments of the human brain. Whether such organoids could develop intelligence—or even consciousness—remains a matter of debate. Professor Lucia Melloni of Ruhr University Bochum, Germany, and Professor Stanislas Dehaene of the Collège de France in Paris propose an experimental framework to answer this question. Their article was published in a special issue on brain organoids of the journal Neuron on Nov. 11, 2026.

medical.title: Shopping for a 2027 health plan? State aid and 4 smart moves can cut your health costs
medical.summary: Residents of at least 11 states who buy coverage through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace can get extra state help paying their premiums in 2027.

medical.title: New guidance outlines use of first immunotherapy for children newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes
medical.summary: For the first time, children ages 8 to 17 who are newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have access to an approved treatment that targets the underlying autoimmune disease, rather than solely managing blood sugar levels with insulin.

medical.title: Rare genetic discovery explains sex development differences in two XY sisters
medical.summary: Two young girls in Vietnam are living proof that there is a lot more to sex than genetics, after being found to have an extremely rare sexual development condition.

medical.title: First complete genomes for neglected malaria parasites revealed
medical.summary: Scientists have produced gold-standard reference genomes for previously neglected malaria parasites by sequencing low-input DNA directly from patient blood, bypassing lab culture.

medical.title: AI used to better predict kidney stone composition
medical.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers developed and tested an artificial intelligence (AI) model that used results from a standard 24-hour urine test to predict kidney stone composition more accurately than a conventional urine-based calculation. Using the AI model, researchers correctly predicted kidney stone composition in 73% of patients, compared with 33% using the conventional calculation alone.

medical.title: Trump administration will fund new research on controversial psychedelic drug ibogaine
medical.summary: Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump.

medical.title: Surveyed cancer patients say cannabis improves symptoms
medical.summary: A new study by the University of Kentucky Markey Cancer Center and the Kentucky Cannabis Center provides insight into how some cancer patients are using cannabis, the benefits they report and how physicians can help patients make informed decisions.

medical.title: Mice help researchers discover how the COVID virus triggers sneezing and coughing
medical.summary: In the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, as Diana Bautista and others in her UC Berkeley lab suffered sneezing and coughing fits and achy bodies, she asked an interesting scientific question: How, exactly, do viruses cause the noxious symptoms we're all familiar with from bouts with colds, the flu and COVID?

medical.title: Smelling Parkinson's: From discovery to skin swab test
medical.summary: A retired nurse who noticed that people with Parkinson's had a distinct odor inspired Manchester scientists to explore changes in molecules on the skin's surface. Using a simple skin swab, they can detect about 15,000 molecular features, approximately 10% of which consistently differ in abundance between people with and without Parkinson's.

medical.title: Combination therapy overcomes treatment resistance in breast cancer models
medical.summary: A combination approach successfully overcame treatment resistance and led to durable responses in preclinical models of advanced breast cancer, according to researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center. The targets at the center of this approach were identified by a new computational biology algorithm developed at UT MD Anderson called TargetScore, suggesting this tool could be used to develop new therapeutic strategies and advance precision oncology.

medical.title: Grief's physical symptoms are real. Here's what you can do to help
medical.summary: Grief can ravage your mind, but science shows it can also weaken your body, leaving you more vulnerable to illness.

medical.title: Scientists identify protein driving age-related organ damage
medical.summary: Monash University researchers have identified a protein that drives age-related damage in vital organs, opening a potential new avenue for treatments that could help people stay healthier as they get older. Published in Immunity, the research revealed a link between the protein granzyme K and signs of aging in the heart, liver and kidneys.

medical.title: College student mental health improves, but significant needs remain
medical.summary: College students are reporting lower rates of depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts, continuing a multiyear pattern of improvement, according to recent findings from the 2025–2026 Healthy Minds Study.

medical.title: Blood thinner could offer a new way to treat osteoarthritis
medical.summary: Osteoarthritis is the most common form of joint disease, a condition that causes joints to become painful and stiff. It can happen to any joint when the cartilage cushioning the ends of bones breaks down or wears away. Currently, there are no approved drugs to slow or stop the underlying disease. But there is a promising development from an unexpected quarter—a blood thinner.

medical.title: Three decision-making styles emerge when people weigh probability words against numbers, researchers report
medical.summary: We don't all understand the same words in the same way, and this can affect the choices we make, according to researchers including those from the University of Tokyo. A team sought to compare how people with an autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and people without ASD interpret probability terms. They found that people with and without ASD could be divided into three groups of decision-makers, whose judgment varied depending on the relative influence of positive or negative framing and the numerical probabilities they inferred from verbal expressions. This work highlights the importance of dialogue to check whether people have understood information as intended and to support informed decision-making.

medical.title: Moderna's RSV vaccine shown to provide strong protection against serious cases in adults 50 and older
medical.summary: A single dose of Moderna's mResvia RSV vaccine was 60.3% protective against documented respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections, 60.2% against RSV-associated emergency department or urgent care encounters and 81.8% against RSV-associated hospitalizations in a population of older U.S. veterans, according to a recent study in JAMA Network Open.

medical.title: Study explores leveraging dental hygienists to expand access to oral health care
medical.summary: Dental hygienists play a critical role in delivering preventive oral health care, helping patients maintain good oral health and preventing more serious and costly dental problems. Yet in many states, laws and regulations governing the dental hygiene profession can limit where and how hygienists practice—potentially restricting patients' access to essential preventive services.

medical.title: New atlas traces how key human brain cells develop before and after birth
medical.summary: Scientists have long known that many developing brain cells originate in one region and migrate to another as they mature. But tracing the molecular changes that occur along that journey has been difficult, in part because some of the temporary prenatal brain structures that give rise to these cells largely disappear around birth.

medical.title: Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk
medical.summary: Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee daily was linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia and better cognitive functioning in a study spanning up to 43 years. The benefits appeared regardless of genetic risk, but decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association.

medical.title: Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect
medical.summary: A surprising discovery reveals how psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms, rapidly reshapes the brain by creating new neural connections and strengthening them. Researchers found that the drug behaves differently in healthy and chronically stressed mice, potentially helping repair brain circuits damaged by prolonged stress. Most intriguingly, they identified a way to trigger this brain rewiring without the behavioral response associated with psychedelic effects.

medical.title: A compound hidden in broccoli could help fight a devastating genetic disease
medical.summary: A compound naturally found in broccoli could help fight Friedreich ataxia, a devastating genetic disease that progressively damages the nervous system, by boosting a vital protein and protecting nerve cells. Scientists hope the discovery could lead to an affordable treatment, although clinical trials are still needed to establish its effectiveness in patients.

science.title: Ultrafast 3D imaging captures fleeting motion at 150,000 frames per second
science.summary: A research team from the Institut national de la recherche scientifique (INRS), led by professor Jinyang Liang, is pushing the limits of ultrafast imaging with a new technology capable of capturing three-dimensional images at speeds of up to 150,000 frames per second. Published in the journal Nature Communications, this study establishes a new world record in profilometry.

science.title: A plethora of seismic eruptions, aka UteQuakes
science.summary: The Utah Utes' rivalry football game with BYU was a triumph for Utah, but it was also a UteQuake extravaganza. No new records were set, but Rice-Eccles Stadium experienced intense seismic shaking during Saturday's game that resulted in a 28–20 victory for the still-undefeated Utah Utes.

science.title: Space telescope Euclid sets the new standard for cosmology
science.summary: On July 1, 2023, the European Space Agency (ESA) launched the Euclid space telescope into space. Its mission: to create the largest and most detailed map of the universe ever made.

science.title: Toxic Salton Sea dust may trigger lung inflammation and reduce gut microbial diversity
science.summary: Though it may not always feel like it, we are a part of nature, and our health depends on the quality of our environmental surroundings. A new study published in Scientific Reports explores a surprising new connection between climate change, pollution and the negative health impacts marginalized communities disproportionately face.

science.title: Sound without physical force creates a sense of resistance to hand movement
science.summary: Virtual reality and augmented reality strongly rely on visual information; consequently, they are inaccessible to individuals with visual impairments. To create illusions of tactile feedback or force sensations without physical contact, previous studies have primarily relied on visual manipulations, such as altering the apparent position of objects, with less attention given to the potential of sound alone.

science.title: eDNA study reveals drivers of dramatic restructuring of marine food web
science.summary: A new study from Plymouth Marine Laboratory (PML) has combined decades of microscope records with cutting-edge environmental DNA (eDNA) data to uncover the drivers of a major shift at the base of the marine food web in UK waters. The work is published in the journal Communications Biology.

science.title: I Am Artemis Katie Spicer
science.summary: For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA. Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the commercially provided human landing systems for NASA’s Artemis program, Spicer will have her handprint on history. Spicer works in the […]

science.title: Two hot zones near Earth's core may fuel volcanoes beneath oceans
science.summary: The ocean covers around 70% of the Earth's surface, but large parts of the seafloor remain largely unexplored.

science.title: Same fertilizer, different timing: Nutrient pulses give two invasive plants an edge
science.summary: Fluctuating resource supplies can help some highly invasive plants outcompete native species. But research on how nutrient fluctuations affect plant invasion has largely relied on greenhouse or simplified experiments, leaving it unclear whether the same mechanisms operate under natural conditions.

science.title: Secret to selling small plates at restaurants: Nonrounded pricing
science.summary: Oh, what a difference a penny can make in the likelihood that restaurant customers will order a small plate.

science.title: Talking or just meowing? Food test suggests cats call for human attention
science.summary: As any cat owner knows, their feline companion is the boss of the home, and their meows are one way to get attention. But are those noises actually an attempt to communicate with us, or simply an expression of how the cat feels?

science.title: Imperfections reveal unexpected links between light and atomic vibrations in ultrathin boron nitride
science.summary: First, one person stands up, followed by their neighbors, one after another, until a wave sweeps through the stadium. Atoms within a material move in a similar way: rather than remaining completely still in their positions, they vibrate together around their respective positions. In physics, these collective lattice vibrations are known as "phonons." Some of them can interact with light and change its energy in the process.

science.title: Zn doping reveals robust two-gap superconductivity in FeSe
science.summary: Researchers using the Steady High Magnetic Field Facility have found that zinc doping unexpectedly alters the superconducting properties of iron selenide (FeSe) while preserving its two-gap superconducting state.

science.title: Digital twins for plants: How ordinary cameras are helping preserve living collections
science.summary: Researchers at the University of Tartu have shown that everyday cameras can create detailed, explorable 3D models of plants, giving botanical gardens and museums an affordable way to document and preserve living collections. The study, by Toivo Aukusti Ylinampa and Urmas Kõljalg, was published in the Biodiversity Data Journal.

science.title: Heart in the Sky at NASA Kennedy
science.summary: The U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds create a heart-shaped smoke trail during a flight maneuver near NASA’s Vehicle Assembly Building during the agency’s MAX POWER expo and air show on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. NASA’s MAX POWER is an aerospace festival celebrating the past, present, and future of flight […]

science.title: Seaweeds can switch to asexual reproduction when there are no mates nearby
science.summary: Kelp switch between sexual and asexual reproduction depending on whether there are potential mates nearby, according to a study by Daniel Liesner at the Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen, Germany, and colleagues, published Nov. 12 in the open-access journal PLOS Biology.

science.title: Chemical traces hint at poisoned hunting weapons in Arabia 125,000 years ago
science.summary: A new study has found people living in Arabia 125,000 years ago used complex technologies, including composite hunting weapons, plant-fiber processing and possibly poison-assisted hunting, while making use of a freshwater lake rich in resources.

science.title: Elephants found to be increasingly isolated, leading to fractured social networks
science.summary: Humans and many other social animals thrive in well-established community networks. Asian elephants are one example of a species that flourishes in groups that work together to access food and care for their young, among other social bonds.

science.title: A new twist on 'magic-angle' graphene: Tuning resistance with strain
science.summary: In materials science labs around the world, researchers regularly reproduce a peculiar experiment. Under a microscope, they use tiny robotic manipulators to lay two sheets of carbon, each a single atom thick, against one another. They then rotate the top sheet against the bottom. The two identical lattices of atoms, when twisted relative to one another, bloom into a complex moiré pattern, a shifting complex of honeycomb shapes that grow and shrink as the angle between the layers changes.

science.title: The diamond paradox: Scientists describe the path to the most stable structure
science.summary: Researchers from Skoltech (part of the VEB.RF Group) and MISIS University have figured out why graphite turns into an unexpected form of diamond under high pressure. Instead of the familiar cubic diamond, the first structure to form is metastable lonsdaleite—a hexagonal form of diamond in which carbon atoms are arranged in layers differently than in ordinary diamond.

science.title: Large mutation analysis challenges claim that evolution shields important genes from changes
science.summary: The idea that important genes mutate less frequently than others was first proposed in 1972 as a challenge to the traditional view of evolution. But the claim has remained contentious. Now, new research from the University of Bath finds the evidence behind that theory to be flawed.

science.title: How human ideas evolve: Technical progress may not require weeding out weaker designs
science.summary: Human culture evolves similarly to living organisms, but unlike biology, human creativity can accumulate improvements at an incredible speed. But how exactly does the process of transmitting and modifying ideas between people work?

science.title: Space dust particles point to ancient heavy-oxygen water reservoir in the Kuiper belt
science.summary: Way out past the asteroid belt, another belt encircles the planets in our solar system. The Kuiper belt, beyond Neptune, preserves icy bodies that escaped much of the processing experienced by objects closer to the sun. Unlike the rocky and metallic asteroid belt, Kuiper belt objects are composed mostly of frozen water, methane and ammonia, mixed with rock and dust.

science.title: Transparency in earnings calls does not guarantee equal access to information
science.summary: The specialized language used by analysts and management in listed companies' Q&A sessions can be challenging for individual investors to follow. However, Kaisa Penttinen's doctoral dissertation in accounting at the University of Vaasa, Finland, shows these sessions still deliver useful information beyond what is disclosed in written reports alone.

science.title: How the discovery of a Roman fort rekindled interest in an emperor immortalized in Welsh mythology
science.summary: The recent discovery of a Roman timber fort in the Preseli hills of Pembrokeshire, southwest Wales, has brought a medieval Welsh legend into fresh focus.

environment.title: US companies apply to explore deep-sea mining in area bordering Pacific island states
environment.summary: Two U.S. companies have applied to the U.S. government for seabed mining exploration licenses in two large patches of international waters near the Cook Islands, Kiribati and French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. Local government officials and environmental organizations are pushing back. The applications are part of a broader move by U.S. companies to […]

[…]

environment.title: Angolan hunters protect Southern Africa’s internationally important wetland
environment.summary: Four years ago, elders from several different communities in Angola’s southeastern highlands approached environmental anthropologist Kerllen Costa, saying they’d noticed an influx of people from outside the highlands coming there to hunt for bushmeat without obtaining permission from local chiefs. Sometimes the outsiders recruited locals to hunt on their behalf. These hunting parties were disregarding […]

environment.title: US brand StarKist suspends tuna sourcing from vessels accused of exploiting Indonesian fishers
environment.summary: U.S. tuna brand StarKist has announced a halt on purchases from fishing vessels linked to forced labor practices in a recent report. It also says it has hired an outside firm to investigate after an Indonesian migrant fishers’ union demanded a binding labor agreement with the company. In a statement sent to Mongabay on Nov. […]

environment.title: Weird and wonderful wildlife revealed in underexplored mountains
environment.summary: A long-term camera trap study has uncovered a treasure trove of wildlife in the Annamite mountains, that run through Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. The mountains have been called the “Amazon of Asia” owing to the huge variety of species here. With hunting and tree loss threatening the area, conservationists are racing to formulate a plan […]

environment.title: Investigation continues in Indonesia after first conviction in 3-ton pangolin trafficking case
environment.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesian investigators say they expect further developments in a major wildlife trafficking case after an intermediary was sentenced to nine years in prison over the discovery of 3.05 metric tons of pangolin scales at the country’s largest port in February this year. “We’re continuing to expand the investigation to dismantle this illegal […]

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

environment.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

environment.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
environment.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

mix_items.summary: ELCEN a finalizat prima etapă a procedurii pentru atribuirea contractului de construire a noii centrale de cogenerare de la CTE Grozăvești, o investiție estimată la aproximativ 600 de milioane de lei. mix_items.summary: Mai multe echipaje medicale şi de pompieri intervin, joi, la un liceu din localitatea Săbăoani, judeţul Neamţ, unde mai mulţi elevi acuză dureri de cap, usturime în gât şi ameţeli, fiind activat Planul Roşu. mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Ultrafast 3D imaging captures fleeting motion at 150,000 frames per second
mix_items.summary: A research team from the Institut national de la recherche scientifique (INRS), led by professor Jinyang Liang, is pushing the limits of ultrafast imaging with a new technology capable of capturing three-dimensional images at speeds of up to 150,000 frames per second. Published in the journal Nature Communications, this study establishes a new world record in profilometry.

mix_items.summary: „Visul meu este să ajung doctor pediatru și să pot ajuta mult copiii”, spune Gabriela, o adolescentă în vârstă de... Articolul Gabriela, adolescenta care visează să devină medic pediatru apare prima dată în World Vision România .

mix_items.title: A plethora of seismic eruptions, aka UteQuakes
mix_items.summary: The Utah Utes' rivalry football game with BYU was a triumph for Utah, but it was also a UteQuake extravaganza. No new records were set, but Rice-Eccles Stadium experienced intense seismic shaking during Saturday's game that resulted in a 28–20 victory for the still-undefeated Utah Utes.

mix_items.summary: Peste 500 de copii au participat la activități de educație nonformală și wellbeing derulate de Fundația Inocenți cu sprijinul Pepco România. The post Sute de copii sprijiniți prin educație nonformală de Inocenți și Pepco appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Tuberculosis rapid test allows in-the-field results
mix_items.summary: Northwestern University engineers have developed a new way to quickly test for tuberculosis that avoids several pitfalls of other methods.

mix_items.title: Space telescope Euclid sets the new standard for cosmology
mix_items.summary: On July 1, 2023, the European Space Agency (ESA) launched the Euclid space telescope into space. Its mission: to create the largest and most detailed map of the universe ever made.

mix_items.title: Toxic Salton Sea dust may trigger lung inflammation and reduce gut microbial diversity
mix_items.summary: Though it may not always feel like it, we are a part of nature, and our health depends on the quality of our environmental surroundings. A new study published in Scientific Reports explores a surprising new connection between climate change, pollution and the negative health impacts marginalized communities disproportionately face.

mix_items.title: Protein guides cytoneme 'highway' formation to support developmental signaling
mix_items.summary: Cytonemes are tendril-like appendages that developing cells use to communicate across large distances. Their cargo—including the key signaling protein Sonic Hedgehog (SHH)—is highly specific, but the mechanisms underlying this specificity were unclear.

mix_items.title: Sound without physical force creates a sense of resistance to hand movement
mix_items.summary: Virtual reality and augmented reality strongly rely on visual information; consequently, they are inaccessible to individuals with visual impairments. To create illusions of tactile feedback or force sensations without physical contact, previous studies have primarily relied on visual manipulations, such as altering the apparent position of objects, with less attention given to the potential of sound alone.

mix_items.title: 7 simple self-care habits that may ease anxiety and depression
mix_items.summary: If you've been feeling more on edge lately, you're far from alone.

mix_items.title: eDNA study reveals drivers of dramatic restructuring of marine food web
mix_items.summary: A new study from Plymouth Marine Laboratory (PML) has combined decades of microscope records with cutting-edge environmental DNA (eDNA) data to uncover the drivers of a major shift at the base of the marine food web in UK waters. The work is published in the journal Communications Biology.

mix_items.title: I Am Artemis Katie Spicer
mix_items.summary: For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA. Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the commercially provided human landing systems for NASA’s Artemis program, Spicer will have her handprint on history. Spicer works in the […]

mix_items.title: How to test whether brain organoids possess consciousness
mix_items.summary: The development of brain organoids is advancing at a breakneck pace. Researchers are creating tiny cell clusters in the lab that behave like fragments of the human brain. Whether such organoids could develop intelligence—or even consciousness—remains a matter of debate. Professor Lucia Melloni of Ruhr University Bochum, Germany, and Professor Stanislas Dehaene of the Collège de France in Paris propose an experimental framework to answer this question. Their article was published in a special issue on brain organoids of the journal Neuron on Nov. 11, 2026.

mix_items.title: Two hot zones near Earth's core may fuel volcanoes beneath oceans
mix_items.summary: The ocean covers around 70% of the Earth's surface, but large parts of the seafloor remain largely unexplored.

mix_items.title: Same fertilizer, different timing: Nutrient pulses give two invasive plants an edge
mix_items.summary: Fluctuating resource supplies can help some highly invasive plants outcompete native species. But research on how nutrient fluctuations affect plant invasion has largely relied on greenhouse or simplified experiments, leaving it unclear whether the same mechanisms operate under natural conditions.

mix_items.title: Secret to selling small plates at restaurants: Nonrounded pricing
mix_items.summary: Oh, what a difference a penny can make in the likelihood that restaurant customers will order a small plate.

mix_items.title: Talking or just meowing? Food test suggests cats call for human attention
mix_items.summary: As any cat owner knows, their feline companion is the boss of the home, and their meows are one way to get attention. But are those noises actually an attempt to communicate with us, or simply an expression of how the cat feels?

mix_items.title: Imperfections reveal unexpected links between light and atomic vibrations in ultrathin boron nitride
mix_items.summary: First, one person stands up, followed by their neighbors, one after another, until a wave sweeps through the stadium. Atoms within a material move in a similar way: rather than remaining completely still in their positions, they vibrate together around their respective positions. In physics, these collective lattice vibrations are known as "phonons." Some of them can interact with light and change its energy in the process.

mix_items.title: Shopping for a 2027 health plan? State aid and 4 smart moves can cut your health costs
mix_items.summary: Residents of at least 11 states who buy coverage through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace can get extra state help paying their premiums in 2027.

mix_items.title: Zn doping reveals robust two-gap superconductivity in FeSe
mix_items.summary: Researchers using the Steady High Magnetic Field Facility have found that zinc doping unexpectedly alters the superconducting properties of iron selenide (FeSe) while preserving its two-gap superconducting state.

mix_items.title: New guidance outlines use of first immunotherapy for children newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes
mix_items.summary: For the first time, children ages 8 to 17 who are newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have access to an approved treatment that targets the underlying autoimmune disease, rather than solely managing blood sugar levels with insulin.

mix_items.title: Rare genetic discovery explains sex development differences in two XY sisters
mix_items.summary: Two young girls in Vietnam are living proof that there is a lot more to sex than genetics, after being found to have an extremely rare sexual development condition.

mix_items.title: Digital twins for plants: How ordinary cameras are helping preserve living collections
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Tartu have shown that everyday cameras can create detailed, explorable 3D models of plants, giving botanical gardens and museums an affordable way to document and preserve living collections. The study, by Toivo Aukusti Ylinampa and Urmas Kõljalg, was published in the Biodiversity Data Journal.

mix_items.summary: The U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds create a heart-shaped smoke trail during a flight maneuver near NASA’s Vehicle Assembly Building during the agency’s MAX POWER expo and air show on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. NASA’s MAX POWER is an aerospace festival celebrating the past, present, and future of flight […]

mix_items.title: Seaweeds can switch to asexual reproduction when there are no mates nearby
mix_items.summary: Kelp switch between sexual and asexual reproduction depending on whether there are potential mates nearby, according to a study by Daniel Liesner at the Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen, Germany, and colleagues, published Nov. 12 in the open-access journal PLOS Biology.

mix_items.title: Chemical traces hint at poisoned hunting weapons in Arabia 125,000 years ago
mix_items.summary: A new study has found people living in Arabia 125,000 years ago used complex technologies, including composite hunting weapons, plant-fiber processing and possibly poison-assisted hunting, while making use of a freshwater lake rich in resources.

mix_items.title: First complete genomes for neglected malaria parasites revealed
mix_items.summary: Scientists have produced gold-standard reference genomes for previously neglected malaria parasites by sequencing low-input DNA directly from patient blood, bypassing lab culture.

mix_items.title: Elephants found to be increasingly isolated, leading to fractured social networks
mix_items.summary: Humans and many other social animals thrive in well-established community networks. Asian elephants are one example of a species that flourishes in groups that work together to access food and care for their young, among other social bonds.

mix_items.title: A new twist on 'magic-angle' graphene: Tuning resistance with strain
mix_items.summary: In materials science labs around the world, researchers regularly reproduce a peculiar experiment. Under a microscope, they use tiny robotic manipulators to lay two sheets of carbon, each a single atom thick, against one another. They then rotate the top sheet against the bottom. The two identical lattices of atoms, when twisted relative to one another, bloom into a complex moiré pattern, a shifting complex of honeycomb shapes that grow and shrink as the angle between the layers changes.

mix_items.title: AI used to better predict kidney stone composition
mix_items.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers developed and tested an artificial intelligence (AI) model that used results from a standard 24-hour urine test to predict kidney stone composition more accurately than a conventional urine-based calculation. Using the AI model, researchers correctly predicted kidney stone composition in 73% of patients, compared with 33% using the conventional calculation alone.

mix_items.title: The diamond paradox: Scientists describe the path to the most stable structure
mix_items.summary: Researchers from Skoltech (part of the VEB.RF Group) and MISIS University have figured out why graphite turns into an unexpected form of diamond under high pressure. Instead of the familiar cubic diamond, the first structure to form is metastable lonsdaleite—a hexagonal form of diamond in which carbon atoms are arranged in layers differently than in ordinary diamond.

mix_items.title: Large mutation analysis challenges claim that evolution shields important genes from changes
mix_items.summary: The idea that important genes mutate less frequently than others was first proposed in 1972 as a challenge to the traditional view of evolution. But the claim has remained contentious. Now, new research from the University of Bath finds the evidence behind that theory to be flawed.

mix_items.title: How human ideas evolve: Technical progress may not require weeding out weaker designs
mix_items.summary: Human culture evolves similarly to living organisms, but unlike biology, human creativity can accumulate improvements at an incredible speed. But how exactly does the process of transmitting and modifying ideas between people work?

mix_items.title: Trump administration will fund new research on controversial psychedelic drug ibogaine
mix_items.summary: Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump.

mix_items.title: Space dust particles point to ancient heavy-oxygen water reservoir in the Kuiper belt
mix_items.summary: Way out past the asteroid belt, another belt encircles the planets in our solar system. The Kuiper belt, beyond Neptune, preserves icy bodies that escaped much of the processing experienced by objects closer to the sun. Unlike the rocky and metallic asteroid belt, Kuiper belt objects are composed mostly of frozen water, methane and ammonia, mixed with rock and dust.

mix_items.title: Transparency in earnings calls does not guarantee equal access to information
mix_items.summary: The specialized language used by analysts and management in listed companies' Q&A sessions can be challenging for individual investors to follow. However, Kaisa Penttinen's doctoral dissertation in accounting at the University of Vaasa, Finland, shows these sessions still deliver useful information beyond what is disclosed in written reports alone.

mix_items.title: Surveyed cancer patients say cannabis improves symptoms
mix_items.summary: A new study by the University of Kentucky Markey Cancer Center and the Kentucky Cannabis Center provides insight into how some cancer patients are using cannabis, the benefits they report and how physicians can help patients make informed decisions.

mix_items.title: How the discovery of a Roman fort rekindled interest in an emperor immortalized in Welsh mythology
mix_items.summary: The recent discovery of a Roman timber fort in the Preseli hills of Pembrokeshire, southwest Wales, has brought a medieval Welsh legend into fresh focus.

mix_items.title: Mice help researchers discover how the COVID virus triggers sneezing and coughing
mix_items.summary: In the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, as Diana Bautista and others in her UC Berkeley lab suffered sneezing and coughing fits and achy bodies, she asked an interesting scientific question: How, exactly, do viruses cause the noxious symptoms we're all familiar with from bouts with colds, the flu and COVID?

mix_items.title: Smelling Parkinson's: From discovery to skin swab test
mix_items.summary: A retired nurse who noticed that people with Parkinson's had a distinct odor inspired Manchester scientists to explore changes in molecules on the skin's surface. Using a simple skin swab, they can detect about 15,000 molecular features, approximately 10% of which consistently differ in abundance between people with and without Parkinson's.

mix_items.title: Combination therapy overcomes treatment resistance in breast cancer models
mix_items.summary: A combination approach successfully overcame treatment resistance and led to durable responses in preclinical models of advanced breast cancer, according to researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center. The targets at the center of this approach were identified by a new computational biology algorithm developed at UT MD Anderson called TargetScore, suggesting this tool could be used to develop new therapeutic strategies and advance precision oncology.

mix_items.title: Grief's physical symptoms are real. Here's what you can do to help
mix_items.summary: Grief can ravage your mind, but science shows it can also weaken your body, leaving you more vulnerable to illness.

mix_items.title: Scientists identify protein driving age-related organ damage
mix_items.summary: Monash University researchers have identified a protein that drives age-related damage in vital organs, opening a potential new avenue for treatments that could help people stay healthier as they get older. Published in Immunity, the research revealed a link between the protein granzyme K and signs of aging in the heart, liver and kidneys.

mix_items.title: College student mental health improves, but significant needs remain
mix_items.summary: College students are reporting lower rates of depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts, continuing a multiyear pattern of improvement, according to recent findings from the 2025–2026 Healthy Minds Study.

mix_items.title: Blood thinner could offer a new way to treat osteoarthritis
mix_items.summary: Osteoarthritis is the most common form of joint disease, a condition that causes joints to become painful and stiff. It can happen to any joint when the cartilage cushioning the ends of bones breaks down or wears away. Currently, there are no approved drugs to slow or stop the underlying disease. But there is a promising development from an unexpected quarter—a blood thinner.

mix_items.title: Three decision-making styles emerge when people weigh probability words against numbers, researchers report
mix_items.summary: We don't all understand the same words in the same way, and this can affect the choices we make, according to researchers including those from the University of Tokyo. A team sought to compare how people with an autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and people without ASD interpret probability terms. They found that people with and without ASD could be divided into three groups of decision-makers, whose judgment varied depending on the relative influence of positive or negative framing and the numerical probabilities they inferred from verbal expressions. This work highlights the importance of dialogue to check whether people have understood information as intended and to support informed decision-making.

mix_items.title: Moderna's RSV vaccine shown to provide strong protection against serious cases in adults 50 and older
mix_items.summary: A single dose of Moderna's mResvia RSV vaccine was 60.3% protective against documented respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections, 60.2% against RSV-associated emergency department or urgent care encounters and 81.8% against RSV-associated hospitalizations in a population of older U.S. veterans, according to a recent study in JAMA Network Open.

mix_items.title: Study explores leveraging dental hygienists to expand access to oral health care
mix_items.summary: Dental hygienists play a critical role in delivering preventive oral health care, helping patients maintain good oral health and preventing more serious and costly dental problems. Yet in many states, laws and regulations governing the dental hygiene profession can limit where and how hygienists practice—potentially restricting patients' access to essential preventive services.

mix_items.title: New atlas traces how key human brain cells develop before and after birth
mix_items.summary: Scientists have long known that many developing brain cells originate in one region and migrate to another as they mature. But tracing the molecular changes that occur along that journey has been difficult, in part because some of the temporary prenatal brain structures that give rise to these cells largely disappear around birth.

mix_items.title: US companies apply to explore deep-sea mining in area bordering Pacific island states
mix_items.summary: Two U.S. companies have applied to the U.S. government for seabed mining exploration licenses in two large patches of international waters near the Cook Islands, Kiribati and French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. Local government officials and environmental organizations are pushing back. The applications are part of a broader move by U.S. companies to […]

mix_items.title: What do a bean and a flamingo have in common? Finding the unexpected in nature photos
mix_items.summary: Photographer Andrew Zuckerman took a moment longer than usual to look closely at a bean that was sprouting in his studio. “There was this one bean that sort of had this incredibly elegant curve, and I thought, ‘God, that’s exactly like the flamingo from like 15 years ago,’” Zuckerman tells Mongabay in a video call. […]

mix_items.title: Angolan hunters protect Southern Africa’s internationally important wetland
mix_items.summary: Four years ago, elders from several different communities in Angola’s southeastern highlands approached environmental anthropologist Kerllen Costa, saying they’d noticed an influx of people from outside the highlands coming there to hunt for bushmeat without obtaining permission from local chiefs. Sometimes the outsiders recruited locals to hunt on their behalf. These hunting parties were disregarding […]

mix_items.title: US brand StarKist suspends tuna sourcing from vessels accused of exploiting Indonesian fishers
mix_items.summary: U.S. tuna brand StarKist has announced a halt on purchases from fishing vessels linked to forced labor practices in a recent report. It also says it has hired an outside firm to investigate after an Indonesian migrant fishers’ union demanded a binding labor agreement with the company. In a statement sent to Mongabay on Nov. […]

mix_items.title: Weird and wonderful wildlife revealed in underexplored mountains
mix_items.summary: A long-term camera trap study has uncovered a treasure trove of wildlife in the Annamite mountains, that run through Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. The mountains have been called the “Amazon of Asia” owing to the huge variety of species here. With hunting and tree loss threatening the area, conservationists are racing to formulate a plan […]

mix_items.title: Investigation continues in Indonesia after first conviction in 3-ton pangolin trafficking case
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesian investigators say they expect further developments in a major wildlife trafficking case after an intermediary was sentenced to nine years in prison over the discovery of 3.05 metric tons of pangolin scales at the country’s largest port in February this year. “We’re continuing to expand the investigation to dismantle this illegal […]

mix_items.title: Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk
mix_items.summary: Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee daily was linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia and better cognitive functioning in a study spanning up to 43 years. The benefits appeared regardless of genetic risk, but decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association.

mix_items.title: Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect
mix_items.summary: A surprising discovery reveals how psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms, rapidly reshapes the brain by creating new neural connections and strengthening them. Researchers found that the drug behaves differently in healthy and chronically stressed mice, potentially helping repair brain circuits damaged by prolonged stress. Most intriguingly, they identified a way to trigger this brain rewiring without the behavioral response associated with psychedelic effects.

mix_items.title: A compound hidden in broccoli could help fight a devastating genetic disease
mix_items.summary: A compound naturally found in broccoli could help fight Friedreich ataxia, a devastating genetic disease that progressively damages the nervous system, by boosting a vital protein and protecting nerve cells. Scientists hope the discovery could lead to an affordable treatment, although clinical trials are still needed to establish its effectiveness in patients.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

mix_items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
mix_items.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
